utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, the Chamber would prefer to you would postpone that. I already explained it in the following way, that there might be a short period in time later this week when the Bench could not be complete, and of course reading summaries is better to do that when the Bench is not complete and -- because the Judge that might be absent would prefer to miss a 65 ter summary rather than a portion of the evidence. Are you -- from -- also from your communication with Madam Usher, I understand that the Prosecution's ready to call its next witness? MR. DI FAZIO: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, the Prosecution's next witness is ready. Mr. Kearney, assisted by Ms. Ley, will take that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Then since the witness has not arrived yet, I can deal with a few more. Mr. Emmerson, you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. I wonder if I might, whilst the witness is being brought in, take stock of the procedural issues which touched upon this witness and the witnesses to follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: In terms of timing and so forth. Your Honours will recall that on the 5th of February of this year we wrote - that is the Haradinaj Defence team - wrote a letter indicating that depending on the outcome of the 73 bis proposals that had been put forward at that stage, there was a category of witnesses for whom it was expected that cross-examination might take longer than usual, and the witnesses for whom we are about to embark fall within that category.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The two witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: In fact, the next three witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Next three witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And probably some of those to follow shortly after. Now, obviously the Prosecution have reduced the time for evidence in chief through the use of 92 ter statements, but I simply wanted to put the Trial Chamber on notice that the nature of the issues that I need to explore with the witnesses to come are likely to take longer than would normally be the case with a witness giving evidence in chief for no more than an hour, an hour and a half, which I think is the current projection in respect of the witness who is about to come. That's the first matter and obviously I'll be guided by the Trial Chamber, and we can take stock of the situation as the cross-examination proceeds. Your Honour, the second is that there are a number of passages in this witness's 92 ter statement to which we take objection in terms of the admissibility of those passages. I can list them on the transcript if that would assist. They are all by and large generalisation about the KLA and their activities which are unsourced and unsubstantiated. They are the last sentence of paragraph 5; second sentence of paragraph 6; the last sentence of paragraph 8; the third and fourth sentences of paragraph 9; and the last seven words of paragraph 11. Some of those passages have found their way into the 92 ter summary which was provided to the Defence shortly before we sat today. So it may be wise, with the Trial Chamber's consent, if the reading of that summary were postponed until Mr. Kearney had an opportunity to consider the position in respect of those passages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kearney, I take it that this has been communicated to you and not yet then perhaps --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It -- it has not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It has not been.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It has not been communicated to Mr. Kearney.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And in order to see whether there's any agreement between the parties on those lines, of course I -- Mr. Kearney, could you please give some priority to looking at it, and of course finally we'll determine the matter once it comes to admission of the 92 ter --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Precisely. I think it about -- I think the nature of the objection would be self-explanatory from the passages I've identified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Again there of course whether it's an admission issue or an evaluation issue is still to be seen. I think we first should turn into private session, if not closed session, in order to further explore the protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In view of the protective measures sought and since we cannot put them in place right away, we'll first go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tomas, you'll first be examined by Mr. Kearney, who's counsel for the Prosecution. And it may have been clear to you that you gave a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. That did not only apply to the initial conversations we had, but of course also for what now will be the core of your testimony. Mr. Kearney, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Mr. Tomas, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: I wonder if you could state your full name for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: My name is Bogdan, last name Tomas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Can I ask you, how do you spell Tomas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Shall I spell it? T-o-m-a-s with a diacritic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Can you please tell us your date of birth, Mr. Tomas.

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: 6 January 1951.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And could you please tell us where it was that you were born.

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: I was born in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Mr. Tomas, I want to talk to you for a moment, if I may, about a statement that you gave on May 23rd of this year, 2007, about one month ago, to representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor. I'd like to ask you, first of all, if on that date did you make a statement to the OTP?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: After that statement was made, was it reduced to writing and given to you for your review?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: It was. It was given to me in Serbian, that's to say the statement that I signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Did you have a chance to read through that document for accuracy to see if it was correct?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: I read through the document, and I wish to state that the document is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: After you made that determination, Mr. Tomas, that it was an accurate document, did you sign the document and initial the pages of it?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: I signed it and I placed my initials on all the pages of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time with the Court's permission, I'm going to ask to draw -- to call up 65 ter Exhibit 1471, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And could we scroll down, please, Your Honour, to the signature line. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Mr. Tomas, do you recognise your own signature on this document?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: I do. That's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Is this a statement that we're talking about, the one that you gave on the 23rd of May of this year, 2007?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: Yes, it is. This is the first page of the statement I gave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Does this statement, Mr. Tomas, reflect what you would say in court today if you were questioned on the same subjects?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: I would give the same answers as I did to The Hague investigators in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I wonder if perhaps we could have the witness take off his earphones for this next portion of my remarks to the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. However, before we do so, Mr. Tomas, could you tell us whether you understand any English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't. I know very little, not enough to be able to understand. I understand very little. I don't think one could possibly know less than I do of a language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Under those circumstances, I think it would be sufficient that you take off your earphones. Could you take off your earphones for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this stage I would normally tender this document through 92 ter, but I do recognise the objections of the Defence in that regard. I have had a chance to look at the passages involved. There are five as -- by my count five such passages, and I believe we can reconcile at least three of them now, and then with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Could we see then -- look at them one by one. We start at paragraph 5 the line: "The activities of the KLA included kidnappings and murders of Serb, Romas and other Albanians who refused to follow the KLA by taking up arms to fight against the Serbian authorities." Would you be willing to take that out?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I believe that that's an accurate statement, but in the interests of admitting this document, the -- we would be willing to admit the following clause in that sentence. The sentence now reads: "The activities of the KLA ..." And I would propose that we insert simply there: "That I was to investigate, included kidnappings and murders of Serbs, Romas, and other Albanians," and I would propose --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Only if that would be the statement of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the witness would be asked whether he was tasked with investigation of these crimes would then -- and if that would then become part of his statement, would that be opposed by Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I have no objection in principle to the witness describing in his testimony what it is he was tasked to do. My objection in each of these passages is to what are essentially sweeping generalised statements which presuppose the very issues that the Trial Chamber has to decide, and given particularly the area where this witness was deployed. These are statements to which I, on the face of them, cannot consent. Now, if what Mr. Kearney is suggesting is that each of them be changed so the sense of the sentence as it appears be changed to indicate it were -- it was a tasking, they're not then the witness's words. The -- each of the passages, as I say, is a sweeping generalisation and statement of fact and it seems to be the right course to simply excise those statements from the 92 ter statement and leave whatever evidence in chief Mr. Kearney thinks is appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, may I reply to that. In the -- in the spirit of good-will, we've offered just now to seek an accommodation with the Defence. However, I would remind counsel, my colleagues, that these are the words of this witness. And it is completely appropriate to explore his words --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But, Mr. Kearney, there's no problem, I think, to elicit such testimony from the witness. The only question is whether these are -- whether these are words that should be introduced through 92 ter. I think that's the only way -- of course there's -- this is not to say that this is not what the witness said, but just whether it's appropriate to introduce specifically this line through 92 ter or whether that should be elicited in another way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And our response to that, Your Honour -- we can certainly go into the matter with the witness. However, these are proper matters, the Prosecution would submit, for cross-examination as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but then it is evidence already. Let's be very practical. I'm drawing now your attention to paragraph 6, the line you mentioned, Mr. Emmerson. "I was sent there because at the time the KLA was committing crimes," et cetera. I read that line as: "I was sent there," and the reasons for which I was sent there was that -- I mean, this is not for the witness to say that this is what happened, but rather he gave the reasons why other people thought he had to go there --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: If I may say so, reading those passages that I've identified as a whole that is an extremely generous interpretation of what the witness is seeking to say. Because if one reads those passages as a whole the witness in our submission the witness is in those passages on the face of it seeking to assert it as fact. For example, the passage in paragraph 9 in the -- in the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On 9 I have a specific question. You said the third and the fourth sentence. Where do you start reading the --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The passage I had in mind was the passage which reads: "He was the cruelest of all" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and I think that's -- is that the third or is that the second?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I read that as the third.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, yes, that is the third --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And the fourth is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- you asked for the third and the fourth. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And so -- and one can see it as well in the last passages in paragraph 8. At the end of the day, these are assertions of a pattern of conduct where there is no evidence in the witness's statement upon which they are based, there is no material which the Defence is in a position to explore, examine, or investigate, and they seek to draw conclusions which are matters for the Trial Chamber in due course to decide on the evidence that is to be heard. My objection in fact goes beyond their inclusion in a 92 ter statement. Unsourced as they are and generalised as they are, I would object to them being given in all testimony. What I wouldn't object to is anything that can properly be admitted with a foundation of fact or, indeed, any statement by the witness as to what he was tasked to investigate. But standing as they do as bleak statements about patterns of crimes and kidnaps which -- without any substantiation or particularisation whatsoever we would respectfully submit that they are not properly to be admitted in any form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, the Chamber will admit the 92 ter witness statement as a whole. And sweeping statements are for this Chamber, sweeping statements, not more, not less. So Mr. Kearney is on notice that if the witness said, Mr. X, Y, or Z was the cruelest of all of them, and I learned that from others, that if Mr. Kearney doesn't further explore that matter, that it's just unsupported, unsourced opinion of this witness. That's the position the Chamber takes; therefore, we do not make it an admissibility issue, but we make it an evaluation issue similar to what we've done before. Because this is not specific for written testimony -- for written statements. This happens now and then in court as well, and I think the Chamber has always taken a similar position. Therefore, your objections against those lines to be admitted are denied.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the same time, the Chamber emphasises that the reasons why you sought the statement, at least for these lines not to be admitted, do not remain unnoticed. Yes, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I did not -- I have not specifically asked you, and perhaps I should have done that. That's a bit of the rhythm in this courtroom, but if I did not give you an opportunity, then -- or whether you would have anything in relation to other lines, please tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the reason that I am on my feet is of course I accept and fully understand the ruling that you have just given. I just did not wish it to be thought that my silence was consent, particularly, in relation to the entirety of paragraph 10 with which I take complete issue in this case. That's all I wanted to say. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that's perfectly clear to the Chamber, of course, that one line goes more against the interests of the one accused, whereas other lines are common. That's fully understood. And then, Mr. Kearney, we could invite the witness to put his earphones on again. Mr. Kearney, you may proceed, and let's just see where we were. No number has been assigned to the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: I was just going to seek to tender it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, the 92 ter statement here we have already the statement in two languages would have number ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit Number P371, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. That is the statement given by Mr. Tomas on the 23rd of May, 2007. Now, we have heard the objections in relation to -- well, the matters we just discussed. Are there any other objections against admission of the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: There are not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There are not. That means that the statement of Mr. Tomas is admitted into evidence, that is then P371. Please proceed, Mr. Kearney.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Mr. Tomas, I'd like to talk to you at this point about some of the interviews you conducted that are described in your May 23rd statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I would like -- I would seek guidance from the Trial Chamber at this stage. We're going to mention the names of people that cooperated in this witness's investigation, they are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think in the statement where it has not been asked yet to have it redacted or to have it under seal, I think at least two people arrested were specifically mentioned. It's -- we offered more or less to the witness that if any of his sources or informants that he would have concerns about the names being mentioned, that he could tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I would simply add that as I think Mr. Kearney is almost certainly aware, at least in respect of one of those named individuals, the summary that he has just put, namely, that this was an individual that cooperated, is not a summary that that individual accepts. And therefore, there would on the face of it be no basis for seeking confidentiality or closed session in respect of the identity of either of those two individuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Whether that is conclusive, Mr. Emmerson, might also depends on if the witness says this and if the person he mentions says otherwise, what to be believe of course and what will be believed by the outside world is another matter. So I don't think that your remarks are conclusive for the reasons you gave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps for in an abundance of caution for the time being we can move in to private session to state their names --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we can do that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Mr. Tomas, how did these two men come in contact with you? How did you first meet them on 7 September 1998?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: These two individuals were arrested by the members of public security during an operation they conducted that day, because these two individuals were armed. I can't tell you exactly where they were arrested, but this is how I came to know them. Because they were brought to the police station, to the premises of the Secretariat of the Interior in Djakovica, and they were handed over to us to interview them. This is how we got in contact with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Do you know when that arrest took place by members of the public security?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: I don't know that for sure, but I can suppose that it was probably on that day. I wouldn't want to speculate any more than this. Normally when somebody is brought in, that person is interviewed on the same day, either by members of the public security or those of state security agency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Do you know if these particular two men when they were arrested by members of public security had been interviewed by members of that agency before you talked with them?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. All I know is that due to the amount of work handled by public security and their inability to interview everyone themselves, we jumped in to interview people, too, because our primary task was an investigative and an operative one. That was our type of work, and this was direct contact with people who were of interest to us. There was so much work that members of the public security were unable to deal with that on their own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tomas, may I ask you the following. The question that was put to you was rather simple: Had these people been interviewed by the others before you interviewed them. Your answer is also quite simple, that you're not aware of that. Then there follows another ten lines in which you explain what would be logical or not logical. If you would first focus on just answering the questions. If Mr. Kearney would like to hear more details or the reasons why you didn't know, he'll certainly ask you. But if on very simple questions you give very long answers, then you stay here for days and days, Mr. Tomas. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I wonder if I might just seek one clarification in respect of the answer at page 71, line 9, and it's the matter that Your Honour's just raised. The witness says in response to Mr. Kearney's question as to whether there had been prior interviews: "I am not aware of that." Now, that could mean I don't know one way or the other or it could mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- that is not something that was brought to my attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time, given the long answer, he tells us all he knows, which clarifies to some extent already the answer. Mr. Kearney, could you also please try to -- to seek answers to be focused on your questions. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Mr. Tomas, just -- very briefly I'll go back on this just before I move on. Do you know one way or the other whether they were interviewed by anyone else before they were given to you for interview?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: I truly am not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And again, when you say "I'm not aware of that," does that mean you don't know? Does that mean you do know? Can you please describe -- explain that answer for us.

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: When I said that I was not aware, I meant that I didn't know. I apologise for the way I'm formulating my answers. This is the first time I find myself in this situation, and I will do my best to be as precise as possible in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tomas, after you interviewed those two men on 7 September 1998, did you make official notes documenting those interviews?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: On the day you mentioned, we only wrote down the summary of the interview -- rather, just the essential facts we gained on the basis of these two interviews. This was written down as a dispatch. On the 7th we informed our centre in Prizren about the facts we had gained on the basis of these interviews.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Sometime after the 7th of September, did you make a written official note of the interviews of both those men?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: Yes. We also wrote down another note in the form of an official note about an interview conducted, and we took a statement from these two persons that was in compliance with the law on Criminal Procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer, Mr. Tomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time I would like to call-up 65 ter Exhibit 1473, please. And if the B/C/S portion of the document can be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Mr. Tomas, do you recognise the document that's on the screen before you?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: This is an official note on an interview. This is a typical note that we write down about the facts that were obtained on the basis of an interview. My colleague and I wrote this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Which interview does this document reflect, please, the interview of whom, sir?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: This note pertains to the interview with Zenelj Alija, born on the 1st of August, 1969, in the village of Kodralija, Djakovica municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: You indicated that the authors of that document were yourself and your colleague. What was his name, please?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: My colleague's name is Dejan Jovovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Does this document, this note as you call it, accurately reflect what Mr. Alija told you during your interview of him in September of 1998?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'd submit that that's an impermissible conclusion at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, the Chamber is not fully aware of -- that it understands your objection, because the question is: "Does this document, this note as you call it, accurately reflect what Mr. Alija told you during your interview of him in September of 1998?"

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I see a number of different and distinct evidential problems with the question as framed. The first one is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we first ask the witness to take off his earphones for a second. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where's the conclusion?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Whether or not it accurately reflects what the witness has told him. It is a note as opposed to a verbatim transcript or copy of what was said. And without some reflection by the witness of the information contained -- contained in the note, the question of the accuracy of whether it accurately reflects what the witness told him at this point is a conclusion. And that's what I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, even under our Rules in a 92 ter statement we always ask whether this accurately reflects what the witness told us, and that's usually on the basis not of a verbatim. So therefore it is possible for someone who has heard the words of the witness giving this statement, especially if someone has then written the note, whether the note of course always in his view accurately reflects. That doesn't mean that there could be no mistake whatsoever. Of course there can be -- at the same time, what is asked from the witness is to confirm that he, to the best of his abilities -- at least that what he did write down, whether that is reflecting what he heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, if that was the question posed, I would not have any difficulty. I wouldn't have any difficulty with how --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's -- let me just try to find out. Mr. Kearney, is that what you meant to ask the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then perhaps --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Then I withdraw the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- rephrase it in such a -- then the objection is withdrawn. Could you please put on -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The reason I'm mentioning this is for the very reason that there was an objection initially with regard to certain names being held in private session. There is a very live issue concerning the entire interview process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do that. At the same time, Mr. Kearney, if you say: Does it accurately reflect ... That question is imprecise to the extent that whether it is a full reflection of -- well, said the core of what was said or whether what is written down reflects what the witness said, which is not the same. Completeness is not answered by this question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Mr. Tomas, this document -- Mr. Tomas, this document that we're talking about in front of you is not a verbatim transcript of what Mr. Alija told you on the date in question. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: This is just the essence of what was stated by Zenelj Alija on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And when you wrote down this essence of what Mr. Alija told you on the date in question, did you attempt to do it accurately and track what it was that he told you?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: Both my colleague and I did our best to portray as accurately as possible what was stated by Zenelj Alija.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: When was it that you wrote this note, Mr. Tomas?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: By your leave, I will briefly explain something related to how these notes are written. The time of the interview is one matter, and quite a different matter is when the interview was described in writing, because there was a shortage of people who could do that and type it. So when it came to typing, normally our notes were dated one day after the interview was conducted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And when was this particular note typed?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: This note may have been typed several days after information was received from Zenelj Alija because there was no time to type it down immediately. Let me repeat that we did not have typists who could type it for us; we had to do it ourselves after completing an interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: May we scroll up on the document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Mr. Tomas, is there a date visible on the upper portion of that document?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: Yes, the 16th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And what does that date reflect, please?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: The date reflects the day when the note was typed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm going to tender this document at this time, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, that would have number ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit Number P372, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections? I hear of no objections. P372 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Kearney.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Mr. Tomas, did you prepare also a note of your interview with Mr. Musaj, this is the interview you had with him on 7 September 1998. Did you subsequently to that interview prepare a note of that statement as well?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to call-up 65 ter Exhibit 1474, please. Perhaps we could scroll down a little further. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Mr. Tomas, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: I do. This is also a note composed by my colleague Jovovic and myself based on the interview with Musaj Ljulj from the village of Donji Ratis, Decani municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: I want to ask you the same question I asked you with the previous document. When you prepared this note did you try to correctly put in it information that Mr. Musaj had given to you on the 7th of September, 1998?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: We solely reflected the information provided by Musaj Ljulj.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And did you do that accurately? Did you try to put down what he had told you accurately in this document?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: We put in solely what was stated by Musaj Ljulj.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: When was this document prepared? When was it typed? I'm going to ask the same question I asked you as to the last document.

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: The document was also typed a couple of days after the interview with Musaj Ljulj.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Could we scroll-up again on this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Is the date that that document was typed visible there on the upper portion of the document?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: As far as I can see -- I apologise. Let me just switch my glasses. This document was typed on the 10th of September, 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Can we see that on the screen with e-court we have I think a cleaner version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have some difficulties in getting the original on my screen in the system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Oh, I have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Kearney.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, at this time I'm going to tender this document as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we have difficulties, not in finding the previous original document in the e-court system, but the present one if I choose the original I have difficulties. But we have it on our screen now in e-court, as long as it's there. So please proceed, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Again, Your Honours, I would tender this document at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, that would be number ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this would be Exhibit Number P373, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Any objections? Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Same for you, Mr. Harvey. It's admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Mr. Tomas --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kearney, I'm looking at the clock. Would it be an appropriate time for a break as far as you are concerned? Then we will have a break, Mr. Tomas, until 6.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And Your Honours, before we break I wonder if I could get some guidance from the Court. I know we had a somewhat of a legal discussion at the inception of this witness's testimony. Could the Court give the Prosecution some kind of guidance as to the timing issue. How long by your calculations does the Prosecution still have left?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll check that over the break and we'll then -- I'll then inform you. We have a break until 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kearney, the indication given by the OTP was one hour and a half. You've spent 49 minutes until now. It's -- of course the Chamber noticed that we have seen more concisely answering witnesses, but -- so therefore we might not be fully strict, but we have to finish our programme this week. So therefore, if that is sufficient guidance for you. I would say if you -- on 49 minutes, that would mean that you would have 40 minutes left. Today we have still got to go for another 56 minutes. That's more than the number I just mentioned. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Thank you for that guidance, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Mr. Tomas, when we broke we had just finished talking about the note you had prepared regarding your interview of Mr. Musaj. Earlier in your testimony you mentioned a -- a third note that you wrote relating to this -- those interviews and the actions you took after them. Is that a fair statement? Did you make a third note in this case?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: That's correct. The note was made after measures were taken on the basis of the information we gained through interviews with these two persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: I'd like to call-up, if I may, at this time, Your Honours, 65 ter Exhibit 1472.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Mr. Tomas, do you recognise the document that is on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Please tell us what it is.

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: This is an official note compiled, written, on the 22nd of September, 1998, which constitutes an overview of all the activities in the period starting with the 7th and in the following days in connection with the information gained through the interviews with the two persons mentioned before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Who is the author of this document?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: The authors of this document are my colleague, Jovovic and I.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time I'm going to tender this document as well, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, that would be number ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit Number P374.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections? No objections. Then P374 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Kearney.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Mr. Tomas, if I have time at the end of my examination today I will come back to these documents, but at this stage I want to move on, if I may. You told us earlier in your testimony about the interviews you conducted of these two men on the 7th of September, 1998. I want to ask you if you are aware of the arrests of other people by state security earlier in September before the arrest of the two men that you just described for us in your testimony.

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question, because we're not talking about the arrests carried out by the state security, and I mean in this instant case; we were talking about the arrests made out -- by the public security.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: I stand corrected. That's a fair statement. I'll rephrase the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I -- can I make a plaintiff plea for Mr. Kearney to avoid leading at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kearney, you are aware -- if you lead you can expect objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And I want to ask you the same question about public security. First of all, do you call public security -- is a short name for them the MUP, Mr. Tomas?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Besides the two men that you interviewed, Mr. Musaj, Mr. Ljulj, are you aware of other individuals who were suspected KLA members that were arrested in early September by the MUP in Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: Can you repeat the question, please. I'm not sure I fully understood it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Certainly. Perhaps I can do this by citing your earlier testimony. This is at page 71, line 9. You said earlier this afternoon: "All I know is that due to the amount of work handled by public security and their inability to interview everyone themselves, we jumped in to interview people." I want to ask you, based -- first of all, to explain that earlier answer you gave. Were there other people being interviewed at that time in Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: Certainly there were more interviews conducted because these were probably not the only two persons arrested on that date. This is my answer to you, if I understood the question correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: I want to ask you if you personally are aware of other people being arrested besides the two men you interviewed, either on the 7th of September or earlier in September of 1998?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: Well, I was not in a position to observe that. We would have the prospective interviewees brought into our office.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: So do you or do you not know of other people being arrested and interviewed besides the two men that you talked about?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: I think I was quite specific. I don't know that because I was not in a position to observe any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tomas, for that answer. I want to move now to a different area, specifically to your trip to the canal that you mention in paragraph 30 of your May statement of this year, 2007. You describe in paragraph 35 coming under attack as you approached the canal, and you describe also a mortar being fired at you. I want you to tell us, please, how long that attack lasted, please, if you can tell us.

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: I will try to answer this question briefly. At one point as we were approaching the location that the two persons mentioned earlier who were there with us were supposed to show to us, a mortar shell was fired at us. It landed and I can't gauge how far it was that it landed. The only thing I know is that the impact was devastating. My reaction was to fall down on my knees, to cower, because I had never experienced anything of that kind before. I know that at that point we were going through a place. On the right-hand side there was an orchard there, I believe it was a cherry orchard. Earlier on we received information to the effect that that particular location had been held by terrorists. The persons guiding us had warned us of having a possible close encounter with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: The cherry orchard you're describing, how close to the canal was that?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: With hindsight I can tell you that we must have travelled for some 20 minutes further before reaching the canal. When I'm saying some 20 minutes, it can be anything between 20 and 25 minutes. I can't be more precise than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Beyond the mortar round that you just described, did you come under any other fire on your way to the canal?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: After the mortar shell had been fired at us, I know that the persons who had been securing the entire mission of visiting Lake Radonjic provided security for us precisely from the right-hand side in order to prevent any such events from happening, and I recall that we were secured from our right-hand side as we were passing by the cherry orchard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: When you say you were secured, what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: That means that a group of uniformed persons ran past us on our right-hand side and entered the orchard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Was there any more fighting that you were aware of after the mortar shell landed?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: To be quite frank, I wasn't able to perceive anything. Ever since that first shell had been fired at us, I had a noise and ringing in my ears, and I wasn't able to perceive anything further.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Do you remember what time it was when you finally did reach the canal?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: I believe it was sometime around noon because the sun was right above us. I also remember that because on that day we were exposed to high temperatures and rainy spells.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: You mention at paragraph 41 of your statement that a videographer came with you to the canal. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: Yes. He was a technician whose primary task was to film what he was able to see in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And after that day, this is 8 September 1998, you've had a chance to watch the film shot by that videographer yourself. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: I didn't see the footage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Have you ever been shown a video purportedly taken on that day, the 8th of September, 1998?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: I saw it once when it was broadcast on the television. This was part of a programme showing what had happened and what had been discovered at Lake Radonjic, but this was something quite short.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Do you have a memory as you sit here now, Mr. Tomas, of what it was that you saw when you went to the canal area on 8 September 1998?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: I do recall that. These are the kinds of scenes that remain etched in one's memory for a long time. As I got there, I immediately saw two corpses floating in the water. To my right-hand side, there was another body that was in a state of decomposition. I also have to say that the two corpses I saw first which were in the water were relatively fresh as far as I was able to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Do you remember when you gave your statement on the 23rd of May of this year, 2007, viewing a video shown to you by members of the Office of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: It was shown to me at the time, and I saw what I had been able to see on that day when I was at Lake Radonjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Did you recognise it as a video that was taken on 8 September 1998 while you were there?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: I recognised -- I recognised in the video everything that I saw on the 8th of September, when I was there at Lake Radonjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I would like to call-up Exhibit P72. I want to play the -- if we may, the witness the first beginning portion of that video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kearney, you keep in mind when to stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to stop there for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Mr. Tomas, this is a -- you've just seen a smaller portion of a much longer video. On May 23rd of this year, 2007, were you shown the entire clip from the 8th of September, 1998, at the canal?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: The video footage was shown to me; however, as far as I was able to see now, this particular clip did not show what I had seen first. The two corpses floating in the water, this was consistent with what I saw first as we arrived at the canal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Do you recognise the clip that you did see as a portion of the longer footage that included those two bodies you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: I have to explain this in a couple of words. We were supposed to be taken by the two persons to the canal at Lake Radonjic. Everything else was the task of the other persons involved in the mission. The technician himself, at his own discretion, decided to start filming wherever he started filming. It was up to him to decide where he would start filming. I had no need to go around, to look any further. My task was of a different nature and it had to do with those two persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Mr. Tomas, I think we have a different part of the video queued at this time. I'd like to play it, just another few moments for you, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kearney, just for the record the previous one was played until 3 minutes, 47. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: May we stop the video there, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Mr. Tomas, do you recognise these bodies that are in the water that are shown on that screen at this time?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: This is precisely the part of the canal, the concrete part, where I arrived with the person who was with me. These are the first pictures that I was able to see as I arrived there. That was the first sight I came across. That is what I saw when I first arrived there, and I remembered what I saw there, that the trousers were dropped down, which used to be part of a police uniform. Another thing that I immediately saw and remembered is that the back of that person was completely black. Otherwise, I remember seeing this body floating with the face down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And that was when you went to the canal on 8 September 1998. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. We came across these two persons. This is how we were brought there, and then everything else followed from there. As we approached, Dejan Jovovic and Musaj, who walked ahead, followed by Zenelj and myself, who were 20 metres behind, we came to the spot from which we could see these two persons -- actually, now on this screen we can just see one of them. Those who walked behind us were just approaching this location.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned in your statement at some point the representatives from the OSCE arrived at the canal, this is in paragraph 45. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: Yes, they arrived towards the dusk.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Can you be more specific about what time they arrived on 8 September 1998, please?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I mentioned earlier that there was rain on that day. I suppose that they were late because they were prevented from reaching that location earlier by the rain, and as far as I could remember, they arrived just before the sun set.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And before I move on, can you just give us any kind of a time estimate as to when the sun set that day, when the -- these people we talked about actually arrived?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: Well, in my view, it's very hard to be more specific, given the time that has passed. But it could have been somewhere between 6.30 and 7.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: I want to move now to a second crime scene that you visited which you described in paragraph 50 of your statement in which you say two or three days later you went to search for other bodies on the road to Dasinovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: May we call-up Exhibit P72, please, and stop it before we actually play it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For the record, Mr. Kearney, the video was stopped before at 5 minutes, 6 seconds, where you asked to have it stopped where the witness said something about the trousers of the body in the canal. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And I'm -- I'm going to -- I would like to begin this next clip at time-period 42, 30, if we may. Thank you. Before we get to that, can we stop it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Mr. Tomas, when you went to the second scene two or three days after you visited the canal, did you again go with the videographer that had been with you at the canal?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: If I need to describe this chronologically and briefly, I will tell you what happened on that day. The shown location is where Dejan Jovovic, Zenelj Alija, and I went accompanied by a reservist -- a police reservist from Decani. The intention was to have Zenelj show us the location where he had personally eye-witnessed the killing of two Serb civilians. He also knew that several more persons, as he said at the time three to four, were killed in that location as well. As he had expressed his readiness to take us there, several days after the Lake Radonjic event, we went to the location in order to find the bodies of those who were killed and buried, those mentioned by Zenelj.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: I want to stop you there. You mentioned what happened when you went to the second location in your statement. I want to first ask you to view a very short segment of this clip that's on the screen in front of you, if we could maybe play it now, and tell us if this is a clip from your visit to that second scene with Mr. Alija.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This clip that is being shown now was filmed at the location which we visited several days after Lake Radonjic. We were taken to this location by Zenelj Alija. He wanted to show us this location, as he was certain that two persons had been killed there; he was an eye-witness to that. In addition to that, he also knew of several more people being killed there. We called this place Ratis, and it is situated somewhere between Ratis and Dasinovac. This is precisely the person, the one on the screen now --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Mr. Tomas --

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: -- this is the person who showed us the location.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: The person who is on the screen now this is at 45.11 in this exhibit. Is this the person you have been describing as Mr. Alija who showed you this site on the date in question?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Does the video that we're watching here document the scene as you saw it on that day, two to three days after you visited the canal?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: Well, yes. That's the video-clip which was filmed by the same technician. There was just that one technician. We found this location and then we informed the superiors in Djakovica, and it was then that this location was discovered. Other technicians came, an investigative judge from Bec and then a pathologist, and there was another colleague there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tomas. Did you just mention that Mr. Alija told you that he personally eye-witnessed the killing of two Serb civilians at this site. Did he tell you who he saw do it?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: In talking to us, Alija told us that on that day, as he was coming back from Albania where he had gone with a group of his colleagues to obtain some weapons, he came across the scene where two people were killed. As far as I can remember, he didn't know the identity of the persons who killed the two Serbs, but he was certain of the location, which he later showed to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kearney. Whom of Defence counsel will be the first to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I will be, Your Honour. And may I indicate we have available for the Trial Chamber and the witnesses -- and the witness a hard copy lever-arch file of material which will be of use with this witness and some of the witnesses to come with some additions to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Emmerson. Mr. Tomas, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Emmerson, who's counsel for Mr. Haradinaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tomas, I want to start --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Excuse me, could counsel speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'll see if that's better for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tomas, I want to start by putting some suggestions to you about the sequence of events that you have described in your witness statement and in your testimony. I want to suggest to you that the two men whose names you have given the Trial Chamber, Zenelj Alija and Ljulj Musaj, were not the source of the information which led you and your colleagues to the canal; that they were, in fact, individuals who were beaten and ill-treated over a period of days in the MUP building in Gjakove; that they were forced by you and your colleagues into signing statements as a pre-text for the search of the canal area, but that the Serb authorities had visited that site before the 8th of September and that the visit which you took part in on the 8th of September was a sham orchestrated for the benefit of the international community to present what was suggested to be a mass grave which was the responsibility of the KLA. That is the suggestion that I am going to pursue with you. And may I invite you, first of all, formally to respond to that.

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: You are inviting me to formally respond to your suggestion which is not consistent with the truth. Up until that moment the Serb authorities had no opportunity or ability to come to that location. That was the first time we entered that territory, as far as I'm aware. At that point in time, given that I had arrived there on the 22nd of July and this was taking place on the 7th of September -- 8th of September, this means that at that point I was already there for five weeks or longer. Let me just add this. Since I was there in the field, I was naturally interested in going further away than Djakovica; however, that was strictly forbidden to us because that area was occupied by the terrorists or, to be more precise, that part of the territory was under the control of the terrorists. Therefore, there was absolutely no possibility of visiting that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tomas, I suggest that that is a lie and that you know it is a lie, and that Serbian paramilitary forces, including the forces of the JSO, entered that area on a number of occasions in the time that you were in Kosovo prior to the 8th of September and that you knew that.

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: It is my position that this was the first entry of our forces into that part of the territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And when you say "that part of the territory," let's just be absolutely clear what you mean by that. At paragraphs 18 and 19 of your witness statement you describe the area which it was not possible to enter as the enter of Lake Radonjic. Is that -- is that what you're referring to when you say "that part of the territory"?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: When referring to that part of territory, I'm referring to the area to the right of the Djakovica-Pec and to the left of the Djakovica-Pec road.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, your testimony to this Tribunal, just so that we're absolutely clear, is that Serb forces did not enter the territory to the eastern side of the road that runs between Peje and Djakovica at any time between your arrival, you told us five weeks before this, and the time you visited the canal. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: I'm giving you the fact that I'm familiar with because it was strictly forbidden to us to move into the territory outside of Djakovica. The only road that we were able to use was the main road from Djakovica to Pec and from Djakovica to Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: When you say "we," Mr. Tomas, who are you referring to there?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: I can speak solely on behalf of us from the State Security Service who had come there to help. Based on what I heard in various conversations, none of the Serb residents of Djakovica was able to move through that part of the territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And by "us," do you include the military wing of the State Security Service, the JSO?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: I don't know anything about the military wing of the State Security Service because I had spent my entire life in the operations service as a civilian working for the State Security Service, nor did I have occasion to see those people at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You never saw members of the JSO during your time in Kosovo; is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: I did not have occasion because I worked in the office.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see. You know -- just so that we're clear, you know that the JSO was the military wing of the organisation you worked for, don't you, Mr. Tomas?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: You're asking me about something that has nothing to do with me. My position was such that I did not have broader knowledge about all of those matters; I was involved in specific tasks only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tomas, the question simply was whether you knew that the JSO was the military wing of the organisation you worked for. Do you know that, or do you have no knowledge about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have knowledge about this, because it was something quite knew for me and it wasn't until I returned to Belgrade that I heard of that, once I returned to my unit. We from the section to which I belonged had no contact and nothing in common with the people that you are referring to as the military wing.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tomas, you joined the State Security Service in 1975, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Are you telling the Tribunal that prior to the time you left Kosovo you did not know that there was an organisation called the JSO which was the military wing of the organisation that had employed you since 1975?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: I can only tell you that I knew of the existence of the Red Berets, who were somewhere in Croatia, and as to learning about them becoming a part of the State Security Service, I only learned about that later. Simply speaking, I wasn't interested in that. I was involved in matters that were of quite different nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Let's just -- let's just pick that up with you if we -- if I may, for a moment. You knew of the existence of the Red Berets whilst they were in Croatia, you tell us. At that time can you confirm, please, the Red Berets were a paramilitary organisation operating outside the state structure. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see. You knew, did you, or not, that the leader of the Red Berets was a man called Frenki Simatovic?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: I heard of Frenki Simatovic. I didn't hear of him being a leader. I simply heard of him in connection with the Red Berets.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see. And that organisation, the Red Berets, which I suggest was operating as a free-lance paramilitary group in Croatia, was brought within the structure of your organisation prior to the conflict in Kosovo, was it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: I'm going to object vague as the time. When counsel says the conflict in Kosovo, that can extend over a broad time-frame.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it is prior or not prior, that's the first question; and then further time-frame could then be established. I think it's a yes or no prior to -- so could you please answer whether the Red Berets were brought within the structure of your organisation prior to the conflict in Kosovo. That's -- as a matter of fact, these are two questions, whether they were brought in, that's one and the second one --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think the witness has already answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you answer the question, please, Mr. Tomas.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What you asked me about the military wing, as you termed it, of the State Security Service, I don't know about that because I told you that I worked in the operations centre which had nothing in common with something that is termed the military wing. This is something that I learned after coming back from Kosovo. I learned that they had been joined with the State Security Service, but please bear in mind that they were a part of the entire sector, whereas I was a part of something that was a lower unit, something called centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tomas, there was a JSO unit stationed in Decan just up the road from Gjakove whilst you were in Kosovo, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: I passed through Decani a couple of times on my way to Pec; however, I don't know that they were stationed there. I'm telling you that the nature of my work is quite different.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You're a member of the intelligence services, stationed in Gjakove in the second half of 1998, and just so that we're clear your evidence is that you did not realise that there was a JSO contingent stationed in Decan whilst you were there. Is that the position?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: It is now my position that I am not aware of this fact because I only passed -- only passed through Decani a couple of times on my way to Pec.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see. Nobody informed you of that fact within the RDB, did they, Mr. Tomas?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: Nobody did, and I don't see why they should have. I was an operations officer. I dealt with specific tasks, and I don't see why I was supposed to know of this, how this was going to be of assistance to me in my work. I don't see the point in you insisting on this when I don't know anything about these matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tomas, I think whether it's logical or not that you're not informed is not the issue. The issue simply is whether you were or not, and your answer is clear, you said, I was not informed about it. I'm looking at the clock, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to adjourn for the day since I have one or two smaller procedural matters. Mr. Tomas, we'll stop for the day. I instruct you that you should not speak with anyone about the testimony you have given until now or you're still about to give, and we'd like to see you back tomorrow, quarter past 2.00, if I'm not mistaken in the same courtroom. Madam Registrar? Madam Registrar is nodding yes. That means that we would like to see you back tomorrow, quarter past 2.00, in this same courtroom. Madam Usher, could you please escort Mr. Tomas out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A few matters. I think we can deal with them without going into private session. The Chamber would like to receive as soon as possible a response from the Defence on the 21st of June, 2007, motion for videolink in relation to Witness 56. When could we expect --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would have thought by tomorrow, certainly so far as we are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: An oral response will suffice?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, oral response to start with would be fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: By tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it would take much time in court, then it usually means that it takes us much time as well to consider it. Then you are suggested to consider a written submission, but the Chamber is not asking for it at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we have -- the Chamber also would like to receive the -- a response of the Defence teams on the 14th motion of trial-related protective measures. That is a limited protective measures, that's only face and voice distortion for a witness who's scheduled for the 28th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: May we adopt the same approach; in other words --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Tomorrow --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- orally tomorrow unless there appear to be substantive objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Since I do not see any objections from the other Defence counsel, that is granted that you respond tomorrow in the way as described. Then we have the -- still the 13th motion for trial-related protective measures for a deceased witness and motion for admission of evidence pursuant to Rule 92 quater which is related to that. When could we receive a response to that motion which was filed on the 21st of June?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So far as protective measures are concerned, I would have thought that the same process might be capable of being adopted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- given the basis for the application. As far as the 92 quater is concerned I think it may be a little longer than that would be would ideal from the Defence point of view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we -- then perhaps the two are related. Would three days -- I mean there's no urgency on the matter at this moment. Would three days do? So then on the 13th motion for protective measures and the Prosecution's motion for admission under Rule 92 quater we expect a decision in four days from now on. These are the urgent matters I wanted to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just before Your Honour rises, might I for one second canvass the question of time. The testimony of this witness on proper examination in our submission is rather more important than it may at first appear. In order to do justice to the cross-examination that I've planned for this witness, I would expect to be some time during the course of tomorrow; in other words, I would expect to occupy, subject of course to the Trial Chamber's view, something in the region of two hours and 40 minutes or thereabouts. I raise it now because if -- if the Trial Chamber wishes at this stage to express a firm view that it ought to be shorter than that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Emmerson, it's always a bit difficult. You ask specific time for this witness. Of course you will have good reasons for that. We do not know, however. So to say now no that would be idiotic --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- to accept would be --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Premature --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- pure speculation. Of course we'll tomorrow, perhaps then at the end of the first session, give you an indication whether we've reached such a verdict on --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: That would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: That would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll carefully listen, and then of course try to do it as efficient as possible -- as efficiently as possible. And at the same time if we would consider it not justified to spend more on this witness, as one would on average expect, we will give you a signal before the start of the second session.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: What I would say is that because the witnesses who follow touch upon matters which overlap with one another, it may be that issues can be raised and dealt with this witness which will be capable of being dealt with more shortly with the witnesses that follows. So some time may be saved so to speak in a swings-and-round-about approach.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just as speculation on our side as the first matter. But I do understand that you make it attractive for us to allow you to spend more time on cross-examination for the reason that later on we'll save more time.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kearney, if you have any specific views on the matters just raised by Mr. Emmerson, the Chamber would like to hear from you, not necessarily at this moment. We are already at 4 minutes past 7.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Perhaps I can express my concerns at the end of the first session tomorrow when we see where we are, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we -- if there's nothing else? Then we stand adjourned until tomorrow, quarter past 2.00, same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
